references.text: Isaiah prophesies that those who oppose the Lord will be put to shame: 'They will be ashamed and ridiculed, all of them' ([ref:Jes 45:16|Isaiah 45:16]). In Luke 13:17, all of Jesus' opponents were shamed when he spoke.
Isaiah speaks about how all who have opposed the Lord will be put to shame ([ref:Jes 45:24|Isaiah 45:24]), which is reflected in the shame of his opponents in Luke 13:17.
On another occasion as well, Jesus' opponents could not answer him when he confronted them with their hypocrisy regarding healing on the Sabbath ([ref:Luk 14:6|Luke 14:6]).
The crowd rejoiced over all of Jesus' mighty works, just as the disciples later rejoiced over all the powerful deeds they had seen ([ref:Luk 19:37|Luke 19:37]).
The opponents were silenced and could not catch him in his words, just as they were also put to shame in [ref:Luk 20:26|Luke 20:26].

The people rejoiced and glorified God's word through the glorious deeds that were done, just as the Gentiles also rejoiced over the gospel in [ref:Apg 13:17|Acts 13:17] and further in [ref:Apg 13:48|Acts 13:48].

Paul describes a situation with both opponents and an open door for service, which recalls the tension between the crowd's joy and the opponents' shame in Luke 13:17 ([ref:1 Kor 16:9|1 Corinthians 16:9]).

Paul writes that the opponents will be put to shame, while believers receive salvation ([ref:Fil 1:28|Philippians 1:28]). This reflects the pattern in Luke 13:17 where the opponents were shamed while the people rejoiced.

Jesus' glorious deeds—including setting the bound free—are a fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy about the Messiah's mission ([ref:Jes 61:1-2|Isaiah 61:1-2]), which Jesus himself read aloud in [ref:Luk 4:18-19|Luke 4:18-19].
